questions.prompt: You changed your website's A record two hours ago, but some users still reach the OLD server. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Resolvers are still serving the old record from cache until its original TTL expires
DNS changes always take exactly 48 hours to propagate worldwide
The old server is intercepting the traffic
The registrar has to approve record changes first
questions.explanation: There's no magic propagation delay — just caching. Every resolver that fetched the old record before your change keeps serving it until that record's TTL runs out. If the old TTL was 86400, some users can see stale data for up to a day. Pro move: lower the TTL well in advance of a planned change, then raise it afterward.

questions.prompt: A host must be reachable over both IPv4 and IPv6. Which TWO record types does its name need?
questions.explanation: A holds the IPv4 address, AAAA (four times a 32-bit A = 128 bits, hence the name) holds the IPv6 address. Clients typically ask for both and race the connections (Happy Eyeballs). A6 was an experimental IPv6 record — obsoleted in favor of AAAA — and PTR is for reverse lookups, not forward reachability.

questions.prompt: Some users resolve shop.example.com fine; others get NXDOMAIN. You query both authoritative servers directly. What's the underlying problem?
accept: the nameservers are out of sync
ns2 is serving an old copy of the zone
questions.answer_display: ns2 is serving a stale copy of the zone (serial 2026073101 vs 2026082402) — zone transfers to it are failing, so it doesn't know shop yet
questions.explanation: The serials differ: ns1 has the Aug 24 zone, ns2 is stuck in July — from before shop.example.com was added. Users get good or bad answers depending on which server their resolver happens to ask. Chase why AXFR/IXFR is failing: TCP/53 blocked to ns2, allow-transfer ACL or TSIG mismatch, or NOTIFY not reaching it. The 'expire' SOA field (1209600 = 14 days) is your countdown before ns2 stops answering entirely.

questions.prompt: dig shows the right answer, but every actual application on this box connects to the wrong address. Where is the bad data coming from?
questions.answer_display: A stale /etc/hosts entry (10.9.9.9) — dig bypasses the hosts file, but applications resolve through it first
questions.explanation: dig talks straight to DNS, but real applications use the system resolver (getaddrinfo), which per nsswitch.conf consults /etc/hosts BEFORE DNS ('hosts: files dns'). getent uses the same path applications do, so it reveals the override that dig can't see. Whenever 'dig is fine but the app connects wrong', check /etc/hosts and nsswitch.conf first — leftover test entries are the usual culprit.

questions.prompt: You just created 'newapp.example.com', but users who tried it a few minutes BEFORE it existed still get NXDOMAIN, while everyone else resolves it fine. What is causing the lingering failures, and what governs how long they last?
questions.answer_display: Negative caching — resolvers cached the earlier NXDOMAIN, and the SOA MINIMUM field sets how long that stays
questions.explanation: A resolver that looked up newapp before you created it cached the NXDOMAIN, and keeps returning it until the negative TTL expires — the lesser of the SOA record's own TTL and its MINIMUM field (RFC 2308). There's no way to force-flush other people's caches, so the cure is prevention: keep the SOA MINIMUM modest (e.g. 300-1800s) for zones that add names frequently. New RECORDS appear instantly; it's the pre-emptive NXDOMAIN that lingers.

questions.prompt: After adding several large TXT records (DKIM keys), lookups for that name started failing intermittently — but only from SOME networks, and 'dig +tcp' always works. What's the likely cause?
choices: Large UDP responses are being fragmented and the fragments dropped on some paths — an EDNS buffer-size problem
TXT records aren't allowed to exceed 255 bytes, so the zone is invalid
DKIM keys must be served over TCP by specification
The resolver is rate-limiting TXT queries
questions.explanation: Big answer + big advertised EDNS buffer (e.g. 4096) = UDP datagrams that fragment at the IP layer, and many middleboxes/paths drop fragments — hence 'works here, fails there', while TCP always succeeds. The DNS Flag Day 2020 fix: default EDNS buffer 1232 bytes, letting oversized answers set TC and fall back to TCP cleanly. (255 bytes is the per-string limit; TXT records concatenate multiple strings just fine.)

questions.prompt: You updated your nameservers months ago and the new servers work when queried directly. But 'dig +trace' and fresh resolvers still hand out the OLD nameservers. Where is the stale data, and how do you fix it?
accept: the parent zone delegation is stale
the ns records at the registrar are old
the parent still delegates to the old servers
delegation at the parent is wrong
fix the ns records at the registrar
questions.answer_display: The PARENT zone's delegation (the NS records at your registrar/TLD) still lists the old nameservers — update them at the registrar
questions.explanation: Two NS sets exist: the authoritative one inside your zone, and the DELEGATION NS records the parent (TLD) hands out — and the parent's set is what resolvers actually follow. You updated the in-zone NS but not the registrar delegation, so +trace (which follows the parent) keeps sending people to the dead servers. Fix it at the registrar; also update glue if the nameservers are in-bailiwick. Compare parent vs child with 'dig NS' at a TLD server versus 'dig NS' at your own — a mismatch is exactly this bug.

questions.prompt: example.com resolves fine on 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1, but SERVFAILs on your corporate resolver and on 9.9.9.9. 'dig +cd' succeeds everywhere. What single root cause explains this split, and why do only SOME resolvers fail?
accept: dnssec is broken and only validating resolvers fail
failing dnssec, non-validating resolvers ignore it
questions.answer_display: The zone is DNSSEC-bogus; only VALIDATING resolvers (Quad9, your corporate one) reject it — non-validators serve it anyway
questions.explanation: +cd (checking disabled) working everywhere is the tell: the DATA is fine, DNSSEC validation is what's failing. Validating resolvers — Quad9 always, your corporate resolver by policy — return SERVFAIL on bogus signatures, while a resolver that isn't validating happily serves it. So 'works on X, fails on Y' isn't flaky networking; it's a real signing problem (expired RRSIG, DS/DNSKEY mismatch). Confirm with 'delv example.com' or DNSViz and fix the chain — don't disable validation.

questions.prompt: You're cutting over to a new host at 02:00. The current A record has TTL 86400. It's now 20:00 the night before. What must you do NOW so the switch is fast, and why won't lowering it at cutover time help?
accept: drop the ttl before the migration
lower the ttl ahead of time
reduce ttl now so caches expire before cutover
questions.answer_display: Lower the TTL NOW (e.g. to 300s) — caches must expire the 86400 record before cutover; a change made AT cutover is itself capped by the old 86400 TTL
questions.explanation: TTL is set by the record resolvers ALREADY hold, not by whatever you publish next. Lowering it at 02:00 is useless: caches populated at 20:00 keep the old value for up to 24 hours. Lower it now to 300s and wait one full old-TTL (24h) so every cache re-fetches the short-TTL version; then at cutover changes propagate in ~5 minutes. Raise it back afterward. This 'lower well ahead, raise after' dance is migration hygiene 101.

questions.prompt: In a Kubernetes cluster, CoreDNS pods keep crashing with 'plugin/loop: Loop ... detected' right after startup. The node's /etc/resolv.conf lists 127.0.0.1 as its nameserver. What's happening?
accept: coredns is forwarding back to itself
loop between coredns and the local resolver
questions.answer_display: A forwarding loop — CoreDNS forwards upstream to /etc/resolv.conf, which points at a local stub (127.0.0.1) that sends the query right back to CoreDNS
questions.explanation: CoreDNS's 'forward . /etc/resolv.conf' inherits the NODE's resolv.conf. If that lists a loopback stub (127.0.0.1, or systemd-resolved's 127.0.0.53), queries bounce stub -> CoreDNS -> stub forever; the 'loop' plugin detects it and kills the pod to prevent meltdown. Fix: point CoreDNS at the real upstream resolvers, or run kubelet with --resolv-conf pointing at the upstream file (e.g. /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf) instead of the stub one.

questions.prompt: In a Kubernetes pod, every lookup of an EXTERNAL name (like api.stripe.com) fires five queries — four NXDOMAINs before the real one. Given this resolv.conf, why?
accept: ndots:5 makes it try the search domains first
search list is tried before the absolute name
the name has fewer than 5 dots so search domains are appended
questions.answer_display: ndots:5 — api.stripe.com has fewer than 5 dots, so the search domains are appended and tried first (4 NXDOMAINs), before the name is finally tried as-is
questions.explanation: ndots:5 means: unless a name contains >=5 dots (or ends in a dot), treat it as relative and walk the search list first. So the pod tries api.stripe.com.default.svc.cluster.local, .svc.cluster.local, .cluster.local, .example.internal — four guaranteed NXDOMAINs — before querying api.stripe.com itself. That's the default Kubernetes behavior (it's what makes short service names like 'mydb' resolve). Mitigations: use FQDNs with a trailing dot ('api.stripe.com.'), lower ndots via dnsConfig for external-heavy pods, or rely on NodeLocal DNSCache to absorb the churn.

questions.prompt: Users behind one central corporate resolver reach a CDN, but get pointed at edge nodes on the wrong continent, adding latency. The CDN uses geo-based DNS. What resolver-side behavior is likely misconfigured or missing?
accept: client subnet is not being sent
questions.answer_display: EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) — without it, the CDN only sees the resolver's location, not the users'; the central resolver isn't forwarding client-subnet hints
questions.explanation: Geo-DNS CDNs place you by the query's apparent origin. When everyone shares one central resolver in, say, Virginia, the CDN sees Virginia and sends your London staff to US edges — unless the resolver forwards EDNS Client Subnet (RFC 7871), a truncated client prefix that lets the CDN geolocate the real user. Either ECS is disabled on the resolver, or the CDN isn't honoring it. Trade-off to weigh: ECS improves locality but leaks client-subnet metadata upstream, which privacy-focused resolvers deliberately withhold.

questions.prompt: On the VPN, 'dig intranet.example.com' returns the correct internal 10.x address, but the application still can't connect and its logs show it dialing a public IP. DNS 'looks fine' from the shell. On modern Linux, what's the most likely culprit?
accept: the app bypasses the stub resolver
resolved is sending the query out the wrong interface
questions.answer_display: systemd-resolved split-horizon routing — the query for example.com is going out the wrong interface, or the app bypasses the 127.0.0.53 stub and uses public DNS directly
questions.explanation: systemd-resolved does per-link DNS: each interface has its own servers and routing domains, so 'example.com' should be pinned to the VPN link via a '~example.com' routing domain pushed by the VPN. If that domain isn't set, resolved may send the query out the public interface and get the external answer. And dig talks to a server directly, while glibc apps go through the 127.0.0.53 stub (or, if statically linked or using their own resolver, bypass it entirely) — so the two can disagree. Check 'resolvectl status' and 'resolvectl query intranet.example.com' rather than trusting dig here.
